# Mediator-relative routing

The two endpoints leave a deeper question: what determines whether an
intervention recruits the public route? The neutral synonym assay compares two
regimes defined by whether article identity distinguishes the intended lexical
alternatives, while keeping both alternatives semantically correct and using
the same intervention procedure. Concrete examples of the two mediator-relative
regimes are shown in @fig-routing A.

All 14 donor-derived directions pass held-out local efficacy. At native
strength, fixed-target-article target-minus-source movement is
\(0.406\ [0.281,0.604]\) logits across six between-class families and
\(0.414\ [0.297,0.555]\) across eight within-class families. Wrong-target
controls yield 0.125 and 0.008; reversed directions yield -0.385 and -0.344.
Intervention-off `a/an` policy mass averages 0.909 (minimum 0.854) and remains
0.899 after intervention. The comparison therefore clears local efficacy and
mediator-support validity without the source-initial conflict of the earlier
prompt construction.

Routing then reverses by mediator equivalence class (@fig-routing). For
between-class alternatives, every family increases the target-article policy;
mean target-article movement is 0.182 and 2/6 switch the greedy article. At
\(\tau=1\), public TV is \(0.176\ [0.108,0.243]\) and private TV is only
\(0.021\ [0.012,0.033]\). Their target-aligned effects are
\(0.189\ [0.065,0.326]\) and 0.019. For within-class alternatives, no family
switches the article and mean policy movement is 0.009. Public TV is
\(0.009\ [0.003,0.018]\), whereas private TV is
\(0.061\ [0.046,0.075]\). More importantly, public target-aligned influence is
approximately zero \(-0.001\ [-0.003,0.001]\), while private target-aligned
influence is \(0.093\ [0.062,0.124]\).

![Mediator-relative route recruitment in Gemma 3 1B. A: between-class synonyms differ in public article identity; within-class synonyms do not. B: each family's signed route contrast \(R=P-H\) has the predicted sign. C: group estimates show both arms of the double dissociation.](manuscript/figures/fig_neutral_synonym_repair.png){#fig-routing width=100%}

The primary signed simple effects support a double dissociation. Between
classes, public-minus-private target influence is
\(0.170\ [0.049,0.296]\), exact one-sided sign-flip \(p=0.0156\). Within class,
private-minus-public influence is \(0.094\ [0.060,0.126]\), \(p=0.00391\).
Every one of six between-class families has \(P-H>0\), and every one of eight
within-class families has \(P-H<0\) (@fig-routing B). The between-minus-within
route interaction is \(0.264\ [0.137,0.399]\); exact family-label permutation
gives \(p=0.00033\). It remains positive at all tested strengths and
temperatures. The group estimates in @fig-routing C show that this interaction
contains both arms of the predicted double dissociation rather than only one
unusually strong group.

The result supports a precise causal statement. When article identity can
express the distinction between two correct alternatives, the intervention
recruits a target-aligned public relay. When the article maps both alternatives
to one equivalence class, token identity cannot carry their lexical difference,
and target-aligned influence persists privately. A generated token is therefore
a lossy public projection relative to the downstream distinction of interest.
We interpret the between-class effect as selective recruitment of an additional
public causal route, not conservation or transfer of a fixed information
quantity between public and private channels.
The experiment does **not** show that a natural online mechanism spontaneously
chooses a carrier: the residual direction is explicitly constructed from named
donors, and between- and within-class sets contain different semantic families.

# Closed-loop gain

Mediator visibility explains which distinctions can travel publicly. But two
interventions with equal local causal strength need not have equal behavioral
effects: a decoder far from its decision boundary is insensitive to a modest
margin shift, whereas a near-balanced decoder can amplify it, especially when
the two continuation branches strongly disagree. Equation 1 makes this
intuition exact. Public effect is local pressure translated through decoder
susceptibility and multiplied by continuation leverage (@fig-gain A). Thus a
feature's downstream effect is not a property of the feature alone.

Across 32 held-out 270M features, article attribution predicts local
intervention-induced margin change (Spearman
\(\rho=0.530\ [0.200,0.772]\)). Attribution alone does not predict public TV
under combined feature-and-prompt holdout at \(\tau=0.1\)
(\(R^2=-0.547\)). Susceptibility alone, leverage alone, activation magnitude,
and a constant baseline also have negative \(R^2\). Calibrating attribution to
local margin pressure and composing it with decoder susceptibility gives
\(R^2=0.827\); adding intervention-off branch leverage gives 0.840, with
calibration slope 0.960. The full composition remains
\(R^2=0.840\)--0.875 across \(\tau=0.1\) to 1. Because `a/an` branch leverage
is uniformly large, its incremental gain over susceptibility is modest; the
task primarily stresses decoder sensitivity. At \(\tau=0.1\), however, rank
correlation is only \(\rho=0.368\), and removing the largest 5% of observed
effects reduces \(R^2\) to -1.34 even as mean absolute error falls from 0.0178
to 0.0113. The impressive aggregate \(R^2\) therefore chiefly reflects correct
identification and sizing of the high-effect regime, not uniformly accurate
ranking of small effects (@fig-gain B; full diagnostics in @fig-app-gain).
The 20 visually near-diagonal effects are not accounting-oracle leakage: every
one has both observed and predicted article-policy movement above 0.9, so both
axes reduce approximately to the same prompt-specific continuation leverage.
None uses the measured intervention margin or numerical clipping. A crossed
feature-and-prompt bootstrap gives a wide 95% interval for aggregate \(R^2\),
\([-0.293,0.986]\), reflecting that these large effects come from only two
sparse features; the result therefore identifies a mechanistically coherent
high-gain regime but does not establish broad feature-population precision.

![Closed-loop gain and held-out prediction at Gemma 3 270M. A: attribution is calibrated to local causal pressure, then composed with decoder susceptibility and continuation leverage. B: the composition captures the high-gain regime; orange cells have both observed and predicted article-policy movement above 0.9, while the inset resolves the low-effect cloud. Holdout excludes feature and prompt identity from causal-pressure calibration; intervention-off decoder susceptibility and branch leverage of the held-out prompt are permitted observed inputs. Aggregate R2 is tail-sensitive and is not a claim of uniformly precise cell-level prediction.](manuscript/figures/fig_attribution_channel_calibration.png){#fig-gain width=96%}

The identity itself is the law of total probability, not the novelty. The
empirical contribution is identifying its mechanistically meaningful factors,
measuring them separately, and showing out-of-sample prediction beyond simple
baselines. The same attribution calibration transfers weakly at 1B, where the
full model is not reliably predictive under combined holdout. We therefore claim
a validated 270M gain account, not a universal predictor.

# Validity stress test at 1B

The sparse 1B campaign illustrates why the ladder's rungs cannot be collapsed.

| Sparse handle | Local efficacy | `a/an` support | What follows? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Frozen top four | No: 0.075-logit mean movement | Yes | No route claim |
| Effect-matched 24 | Yes | No: `called` often dominates | No binary route claim |
| Constrained frontier | Yes | Yes: 20/20 prompts | Low-amplitude hybrid route |

These distinct outcomes---weak handle, support-invalid estimand, and valid
hybrid route---would be conflated by reporting only free generation.
Reconstruction and graph-coverage audits reduce, but do not remove,
instrumentation uncertainty. We use this campaign as a validity demonstration,
not evidence that scale reorganizes sparse planning mechanisms.
